paras: The lynching of Bees was the killing of a Black man by a mob near the Leake plantation at Rosetta, Mississippi, at the end of August or on September 1, 1905. He was charged with an attempted criminal assault on a white girl, and the news reached papers across the country only as brief wire items. The single Black-press notice found was one sentence in a weekly news digest.

The reports give no background beyond the accusation: the man, called "a negro named Bees," was charged with attempting a "criminal assault upon a white girl." According to a Memphis dispatch, the girl was the daughter of a planter near Rosetta, aged seven in the Paducah Sun's version and "only ten years old" in another. No first name, age or occupation for him appears in the coverage, and his surname was also printed as Rees, Beese, Beesly and Beas.

The Associated Press dispatch from Rosetta, dated September 1, said only that word had reached the town that Bees "has been lynched by a mob near Leake plantation." Memphis reports of the same date put the lynching on the previous night, August 31, while a shorter Rosetta item in the New York Evening World said it took place "this afternoon," September 1. None of the accounts describes how he was killed, who made up the mob or how large it was.
No report of an arrest, inquest or official response was found, and no Mississippi paper's account of the lynching turned up in the coverage.

White papers from New York to Montana carried the story between September 1 and mid-September, most as the bare wire text under headings such as "Mississippi Negro Lynched." Headline writers often treated the charge as proven: the Rock Island Argus ran "Negro Assailant of White Girl Lynched," the Vinita Daily Chieftain "Brutal Negro Assaults White Girl and is Lynched," and the Ottumwa Courier "Negro is Killed by a Mob For Attempting Brutal Crime." The Paducah Sun headed its Memphis item "The Usual Punishment Meted Out For the Usual Crime," and the Evening World's short version stated flatly that "He had attacked a white girl."

The qualifier in the wire text shifted as the story was reprinted. The Daily Tribune's Memphis item called it "the alleged attempt at assault," whereas a Montana weekly's digest dropped "attempted" and said he was "charged with criminal assault." In the Black press, the Wichita Searchlight gave the lynching one sentence in its "Latest News in Brief" column on September 9, worded exactly as in a white Kansas weekly's digest that day, with no headline or comment.

The accounts differ on the date, falling on the night of August 31 in the Memphis reports and the afternoon of September 1 in the Evening World item. They also differ on the girl's age, given as seven or ten, and the Daily Ardmoreite called her "a white woman."

reader.title: Lynching of Bees
bases: Every report says a mob or unnamed parties 'lynched' a Black man accused of an attempted assault on a white girl near Rosetta, Mississippi (A2, A6, A7).

Two separate dispatches (Rosetta and Memphis datelines) report that a Black man was 'lynched by a mob' over an accusation of attempted assault on a white girl, with no legal proceeding mentioned (A2, A6, A7); a mob killing as punishment for an alleged crime meets the standard definition.

A Rosetta-datelined wire (A2, A3) and a Memphis-datelined report with different details (A6, A7) agree that a Black man named Bees or a similar name was lynched near Rosetta over an alleged attempted assault on a white girl, though no local Mississippi account was found.
